clue: Before this development, moving products like food, cloth, and tools across the country took many months and was very expensive. Farmers, miners, and factory owners struggled to get their goods to customers on the other side of the country. Once this was completed, businesses could ship products from coast to coast in about a week, transforming the American economy.

This company was one of the two railroads that built the Transcontinental Railroad, and it started building from the east. Its workers, many of them Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans, laid tracks heading west across the flat Great Plains. It began its route in Omaha, Nebraska, and raced to lay as many miles of track as possible.

This was a famous, difficult obstacle that workers on the Central Pacific Railroad could not go around and had to go through. Using explosives like black powder and a new chemical called nitroglycerin, workers carved a path through solid rock. This enormous range of mountains in California tested the railroad builders more than any other part of the route.

This group of workers was hired by the Central Pacific Railroad and made up a large portion of the railroad's workforce. They came from a country in East Asia and were known for working incredibly hard through dangerous mountain terrain. They were paid less than other workers, but helped blast and carve the railroad through the Sierra Nevada mountains in California.

This invention worked alongside the transcontinental railroad and helped connect the country in a different way — through communication instead of transportation. Wires were strung along the railroad's route as it was being built, allowing messages to travel coast to coast almost instantly. When the final spike was struck in 1869, this technology carried the news to the rest of the nation in seconds.

This remote location in the American West became famous for a single day in May 1869. Two massive construction crews, one working from the east and one from the west, were racing toward each other for years before they finally met here. It is the place where the last spike of the transcontinental railroad was driven and the continent was connected by rail for the first time.

This object was driven into the ground at a special ceremony to mark the completion of the transcontinental railroad. Unlike ordinary railroad spikes, this one was made from a precious metal and became a symbol of the great achievement. A telegraph was connected to it so that when it was tapped with a hammer, the whole country would instantly know the railroad was done.

This man was the governor of California and one of the four businessmen who helped found the Central Pacific Railroad. He was so important to the project that he was given the honor of driving the final spike into the ground at the completion ceremony. He later used his fortune to found one of the world's most famous universities in California, which still bears his family's name today.
